source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Rapidly rewarm the fingers in circulating water at about 37-39°C.","B":"Massage the frozen fingers vigorously while warming.","C":"Apply a heating pad directly to numb tissue.","D":"Let the fingers thaw slowly at room temperature despite a controlled warm-water bath."}}
source_row.rationale: WMS recommends rapid water-bath rewarming at 37-39°C when thawing can be maintained and refreezing prevented. Option A is correct. Rubbing and direct dry heat can worsen tissue injury, while slow room-temperature thawing is inferior when controlled rapid rewarming is available.
source_row.source_detail: Field/clinical rewarming: when thawing can be maintained and refreezing prevented, rapidly rewarm frostbite in circulating water at 37-39°C; avoid rubbing/massage and direct dry heat, and protect thawed tissue from refreezing and trauma. WMS Frostbite Clinical Practice Guideline Summary 2024; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, emergency response and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

source_row.stem: A client with frostbitten fingers arrives where refreezing can be prevented. Which rewarming method is appropriate?
